The SSEBFF package is designed to assist in sample size estimation for clinical trials across various paradigms, including frequentist, Bayesian, and Non-inferiority. This vignette focuses on the frequentist paradigm.

\section*{Introduction}
Sample size estimation is a critical step in the design of clinical trials. The SSEBFF package provides tools for estimating sample sizes in frequentist clinical trial designs.

In frequentist paradigms, sample size estimation typically involves determining the number of participants needed to achieve a specified level of statistical power, given a hypothesized effect size and significance level. The package includes functions that allow users to perform these calculations for various types of clinical trials, including those with binary and continuous outcomes.

The hypothesis testing framework used in frequentist paradigms relies on the concept of null and alternative hypotheses. In one-arm practicing, the null hypothesis typically states that the treatment has no effect ($H_0$: $\theta \le \theta^* $, where $ \theta^* $ is the threshold and is also depicted as $\theta_0$ or $\Delta$), while the alternative hypothesis posits that the treatment does have an effect.($H_a$: $\theta > \theta^* $) The sample size is calculated to ensure that the trial has sufficient power to detect a true effect if it exists. While in two-arm, the null hypothesis states that there is no difference between the two treatment groups($H_0$: $\theta_T = \theta_C$, where $\theta_T$ is the treatment group parameter, and $\theta_C$ is the control group parameter), and the alternative hypothesis states that there is a difference($H_a$: $\theta_T \ne \theta_C$).

```{r setup}
library(SSEBFF)
```
We will demonstrate the package function through example simulations. In this package we provide a combined function for sample size estimation for both one-arm and two-arm trials, which can be used to estimate the sample size needed to achieve a specified power and significance level.
